title: David Prepares for the Temple and Charges Solomon
summary: David declares Ornan's threshing floor the site of the LORD's house and begins gathering stone, iron, bronze, and cedar in vast amounts. He tells Solomon that God forbade David to build because he had shed much blood, but promised a son who would be a man of rest. David charges Solomon to keep God's law, be strong and courageous, and build, and he commands Israel's leaders to help him.
story: Chapter 21 ended at an altar on Ornan's threshing floor. This chapter opens with David naming it: here shall be the house of the LORD God. From now until the end of 1 Chronicles, the story turns entirely to the temple. David cannot build it, as God said in chapter 17, but the Chronicler shows him doing everything short of building: gathering materials, organizing workers, charging his son, and enlisting the leaders. Chapters 23 to 27 will organize the Levites, priests, musicians, gatekeepers, and officials, and chapters 28 and 29 will hand everything over to Solomon. The temple will be Solomon's building, but in Chronicles it is David's vision.
historical:
The 1 Kings account has Solomon doing the temple preparations (1 Kings 5), with little about David's role. Chronicles gives David a large share, presenting him as the temple's founder in all but construction. This emphasis suited the Chronicler's first readers in the Persian period, who worshiped in the rebuilt second temple, completed around 516/515 BC. By tracing its worship back to David, the Chronicler gave their modest temple a place in the promise to David.

The foreigners conscripted as stonecutters (verse 2) were non-Israelite residents of the land; 2 Chronicles 2:17-18 describes Solomon counting and assigning them in the same way. Sidon and Tyre, the great Phoenician cities, supplied the cedar (verse 4), continuing the relationship begun with Hiram in chapter 14.
cultural:
The quantities in verse 14 are immense: 100,000 talents of gold and a million talents of silver. With a talent commonly estimated at around thirty kilograms, the gold alone would weigh about three thousand metric tons, far beyond what any ancient kingdom is known to have possessed. Interpreters handle this in different ways: as royal hyperbole of a kind common in ancient inscriptions, as a copying problem with numbers, or as a unit of measure different from the one usually assumed. The Chronicler's point is plain either way: David gave lavishly, more than could be weighed or counted.

The charge to be strong and courageous is the formula of leadership transition in Israel's story, spoken to Joshua when he succeeded Moses (Deuteronomy 31:7-8; Joshua 1:6-9). Using it here casts Solomon as a new Joshua, completing what his predecessor began and bringing Israel into rest.
literary: The chapter has three movements: David's preparations (verses 1-5), David's private charge to Solomon (verses 6-16), and his public charge to the leaders (verses 17-19). The charge to Solomon retells God's promise from chapter 17 with new details: the reason David may not build, the meaning of Solomon's name, and the promise of rest and peace. The name Solomon (Shelomoh) sounds like shalom, peace, and verse 9 plays on it: his name will be Solomon, and I will grant to Israel peace and quiet during his reign. Key words recur: rest, the house for My Name, be strong, and the LORD be with you. The whole speech sounds like Moses' farewell to Joshua, a deliberate echo.

outline.t: Here shall be the house of the LORD
Why David cannot build, and the son of rest

doctrines.note: The temple is to be exceedingly magnificent because it is the house of the LORD. David's lavish preparation reflects the worth of the one to be worshiped there.

Solomon's success is tied to keeping the Law of the LORD and the statutes Moses received (verses 12-13). Building the temple is not a substitute for obedience; the king's first task is to keep God's word.
David repeats God's promise: He will be My son, and I will be his Father, and his throne will be established forever. The Davidic covenant of chapter 17 now directs the next generation.
The temple is linked to rest from enemies (verses 9 and 18). In Chronicles, God's dwelling among his people and their security in the land belong together.

words.note: Menuchah, rest or resting place. Solomon is called a man of rest (verse 9). Rest in the Old Testament means security from enemies in the land God gave, a theme running from Deuteronomy 12:9-10 through Joshua. The temple is built when God grants that rest.

Shalom, peace, wholeness, well-being. It is more than the absence of war; it is things as they should be. Verse 9 connects it with Solomon's name. The king of peace, not the warrior king, builds the house of God.

Kun, to prepare or establish. David prepared materials in abundance (verses 3, 5, 14). The same verb is used for God establishing David's throne. David prepares a house for God, while God establishes a house for David.
Amats, to be strong or courageous, paired with chazaq in verse 13. The pair is the language of Moses' commission of Joshua. It calls for steady resolve under a heavy task, grounded in God's presence.

christ: The chapter's links to Christ run through the son of David who builds God's house and reigns in peace. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one who builds God's true temple, a people in whom God dwells (1 Peter 2:5; Ephesians 2:21-22), and as the Prince of Peace promised in Isaiah 9:6. Hebrews 4 speaks of a rest that remains for God's people beyond the rest Joshua gave, a rest Christians find in Christ. The pattern of a father who prepares and a son who completes the work also echoes, loosely, Jesus' words about finishing the work his Father gave him (John 17:4). These are thematic connections the New Testament makes, not predictions in the chapter itself.

hard.q: Why was David forbidden to build the temple because he had shed blood, when God gave him his victories?
hard.a: The chapter credits God with David's victories (18:6, 13) and then says his bloodshed disqualified him from building. Some interpreters take this as a moral judgment, with David's wars, however necessary, leaving a stain unsuitable for a house of peace. Others see it as ritual or symbolic rather than moral: the temple was to be built in a time of rest, by a king whose reign embodied peace, so that the building would express what God intended for his people. Still others note that David's personal bloodshed included the killing of Uriah, though Chronicles doesn't mention it. What the chapter makes clear is that David accepted the limit and spent his energy preparing for someone else to finish the work.

questions: David spent his last years preparing for a building he would never see. What are you preparing that someone else may finish?
Solomon's success depended on keeping God's law more than on the materials David gathered. Where are you tempted to trust resources more than faithfulness?
Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or discouraged. What task in your life needs that charge right now?
